title: Pawn Structure and Holes
subtitle: Backward pawns create targets; holes create outposts

source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter VI, §31 Some Salient Points About Pawns, unnumbered diagram conventionally associated with Example 63

narration.say: This diagram studies pawns only. The original omits both kings. Here they are placed on h1 and h8 solely so the rules engine can load the position.
Do not analyse this as a complete endgame. We are studying targets and squares, not calculating a result.
Black’s pawn on c7 is backward. White’s pawn on d4 controls its advance to c5.
There are no white pawns on the c-file. In a position with rooks, White could concentrate pressure along that file.
The square c5 is supported by the pawns on b4 and d4.
Black has no b-pawn or d-pawn that can attack a white piece established on c5. Removing that piece would require a piece exchange rather than a pawn attack.
White’s pawn on e5 supports f6. Black’s e-pawn and g-pawn are already on the sixth rank and cannot drive a piece away from f6.
This is a hole in the pawn cover: a square that opposing pieces may occupy without being challenged by those pawns.

steps.title: Read the pawn skeleton before choosing a plan

narration.say: A backward pawn provides a target. A hole provides a potential outpost.
In a complete position, piece placement determines how those weaknesses can be exploited. The pawn diagram alone does not establish a forced win.
There are no move exercises in this lesson: adding a tactical solution would invent information absent from the source.
